items.title: Mary Miss’s Long Fight to Keep Public Art Alive
items.summary:
In the early decades of postwar America, public art tended to be seen as the pallid stepchild of architecture and design. Steel, bronze, or stone abstractions sited in front of modernist buildings were denigrated as “plop art,” or even more damningly as “the turd in the plaza.” And, accordingly, public artists were relegated to the province of decoration or historical commemoration while public responses to their art ranged from indifference to outrage over the expenditure of public money.

Then, in the 1980s, public art was jolted by a revolution. Rebelling against the tradition of the static monument, a group of young artists aspired instead to explore how art in public spaces could encourage connection, reflection, and interaction among viewers who didn’t necessarily have an art education. They created mazes, placed mirrors in the landscape, and drew lines in the snow. An extension of the boundary-breaking experiments of avant-garde artists of the 1970s, this new public art slowly began to gain acceptance from funders, developers, government officials, and general audiences.

South Cove , 1984–87, designed by Mary Miss, in collaboration with landscape architect Susan Child and architect Stanton Eckstut, in Battery Park City, New York. 

Courtesy Hugh L. Carey Battery Park City Authority and Mary Miss 

Among the most adventurous of these pioneers was Mary Miss. Raised in the American West, she was interested in the tensions between rural and urban landscapes, the built and unbuilt environment, and the ways in which people navigate their path through the spaces of the…
items.t: Mary Miss’s Long Fight to Keep Public Art Alive

items.title: EU Countries Renew Call To Exclude Russia from Venice Ahead of 2027 Architecture Biennale
items.summary:
Ten European Union countries are demanding “further and sustained efforts” from the European Commission to keep Russia out of the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennial, according to Rapporteur .

The report cites a diplomatic note signed by Poland, Austria, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, and Sweden, which says Moscow’s presence on the prestigious cultural stage risks normalizing its war on Ukraine. “In light of the current geopolitical realities… there should be no room for ‘normalisation’ of Russia’s participation in international sporting and cultural events, as long as there is no just and lasting peace in Ukraine,” the note reportedly reads. The group urged the European Union to take measures against Russia’s participation ahead of a meeting of EU culture ministers on Thursday and Friday.

Russia returned to the Venice Biennale in May for the first time since invading Ukraine in 2022, to the condemnation of politicians, artists, and cultural workers worldwide. (In 2024, Russia did not participate, choosing instead to lend its pavilion to Bolivia, which does not have a dedicated exhibition space on the Biennale grounds.)

An open letter circulating this year addressed Biennale president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco directly. “The claim that ‘culture is above politics’ is never neutral. In the case of contemporary Russia, this formula has become a political instrument used to promote aggression and advance state agendas while disguising them behind the language of cultural exchange and dialogue,” the letter read. It was signed by Pina Picierno, an…
items.t: EU Countries Renew Call To Exclude Russia from Venice Ahead of 2027 Architecture Biennale

items.title: Kelly Gough is simply astounding as Desire Under the Elms reaches the heights of Greek tragedy
items.summary:
Almeida theatre, London
Part-Phaedra and part-Medea, Gough is mesmerising in Ebenezer Bamgboye’s stylised staging of Eugene O’Neill’s family drama

You would not know that Eugene O’Neill’s play was originally set on a mid 19th-century farm. This version by director Ebenezer Bamgboye brings modernity with its sleek storytelling, but also nods to the ancient Greek drama O’Neill was emulating in his 1924 play about illicit desire and the father-son fight for land.

It makes for a strange mix at first, beguiling and bewildering in equal measure. Bamgboye employs some of the striking theatricality that he brought to his magnetic adaptation of The Lonely Londoners two years ago. It is an original refashioning, the script sharper with less of the exposition that might date it, but the directorial flourishes come so thick and fast that it is stylised to the bone. Bamgboye has previously worked with Rebecca Frecknall (who staged the leaden O’Neill drama A Moon for the Misbegotten last year) and the first half seems to pay too big a debt to her style of work.

Continue reading...
items.t: Kelly Gough is simply astounding as Desire Under the Elms reaches the heights of Greek tragedy

items.title: UK Culture Secretary Faces Scrutiny After British Council’s Donation to Palestinian Museum
items.summary:
The British Council came under fire from a pro-Israel lobbying group after providing public funding to the Palestinian Museum in Birzeit, West Bank, reports the Telegraph .

Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, received a letter from UK Lawyers for Israel (UKLFI), saying that supporting such a cause “concerned that UK public money” and “glorifies terrorist activity.” ARTnews reached out to UKLFI at the time of press for the contents of the letter and whether Nandy’s office had responded.

According to the Telegraph , the British Council’s Cultural Protection Fund has provided Taawon UK, a Palestinian-led charity linked to the Palestinian Museum, with numerous grants since 2018 with the aim of “support heritage projects in the West Bank and Jerusalem.” The museum was opened in 2016, and UKLFI is calling on the government to halt any fundings as its exhibitions “present people responsible for some of the deadliest terrorist attacks on Israeli civilians as heroes, martyrs and freedom fighters, without mentioning their victims.” 

Among them objects exhibited there have been posters depicting Dalal al-Mughrabi, who led the 1978 Coastal Road massacre in which 38 Israelis were killed, as a martyr, alongside material celebrating Hamas bombmaker Yahya Ayyash.

In 2019, the Palestinian Museum received a grant of £152,208 through Taawon UK. The award notice stated that the museum conserve and digitize comments “complemented by a wide range of advocacy and education activities hosted by the Palestinian Museum.” 

Taawon UK’s funds have come under further inspection, as UKLFI wrote to…
items.t: UK Culture Secretary Faces Scrutiny After British Council’s Donation to Palestinian Museum

items.title: Wyoming Art Dealer Sentenced After Falsely Claiming Native American Heritage
items.summary:
Jose Martinez, who adopted the name Joseph Skywolf while he ran Skywolf’s Gallery in Jackson, Wyoming, has been sentenced after pleading guilty to a felony charge of falsely representing himself as Native American and claiming certain offerings were created by Native American artists or tribes.

According to the US Department of the Interior, Martinez violated the Indian Arts and Crafts Act, PL 101-644, while working at the namesake of Skywolf’s in 2023 and 2024. “Martinez offered or displayed for sale various kinds of artwork, such as headdresses, jewelry, paintings, and beaded tanned hides, that he falsely represented as made by an Indian or by a specific Indian Tribe,” reads a statement from the Department of the Interior. He has been sentenced to 24 months of supervised probation and ordered to pay $14,100 in restitution.

“Authentic Indian art and craftwork is an important tool for passing down cultural traditions and artistic skills from one generation to the next,” said Meridith Stanton, director of the Department of the Interior’s Indian Arts and Crafts Board (IACB). “While falsely claiming to be Chiricahua Apache, Apache, Navajo, and Native American when selling his counterfeit Indian art, Martinez undercut authentic Indian artists and Indian economies, culture, and traditions.”

The director added a warning to others who might follow Martinez’s path: “For those selling counterfeit Indian art and craftwork it is important to know that wherever you are we will diligently work to find you and prosecute you under the Indian Arts and Crafts Act.”
items.t: Wyoming Art Dealer Sentenced After Falsely Claiming Native American Heritage

items.title: Billionaire Collector Ken Griffin Loans Three Dinosaur Fossils to Pittsburgh Museum
items.summary:
Kenneth C. Griffin, the billionaire collector known for buying everything from Abstract Expressionist paintings to rare copies of the US Constitution, will loan three dinosaur fossils to Pittsburgh’s Carnegie Museum of Natural History.

The fossils—nicknamed “Daisy,” “Lucky,” and “Lucy”—are all sauropods, according to the Financial Times , which also reported that Griffin will gift the museum $5 million in support of its education programming. The gift will also enable the museum to launch a paleontology lab that will be viewable to the public every day.

“Daisy, Lucky and Lucy offer an extraordinary window into our planet’s history,” Griffin said in a statement. “I am proud to partner with the Carnegie Museum of Natural History to share these remarkable dinosaurs with the public and give visitors a front-row seat to the work of paleontologists.”

All three fossils date to the Jurassic Period and were found between 2023 and 2025 in Washakie County, Wyoming, per the Financial Times . No financial value for these fossils has ever been publicly reported, but it’s possible that they are not even the most expensive ones owned by Griffin, a mainstay of the ARTnews Top 200 Collectors list since 2007.

In 2024, he memorably purchased a stegosaurus nicknamed “Apex” at a Sotheby’s auction in 2024. When it appeared there, the house billed it as the second-most complete Stegosaurus fossil ever discovered. Griffin bought it for $44.6 million, a record at the time for the most expensive dinosaur fossil ever brought to a public auction. Not long after buying “Apex,” Griffin loaned the…
items.t: Billionaire Collector Ken Griffin Loans Three Dinosaur Fossils to Pittsburgh Museum

items.title: Eleanor Antin Sues Dealer for Withholding Nearly 200 Works
items.summary:
Conceptual artist Eleanor Antin is seeking the return of at least 179 works or $975,000 in compensatory damages in a lawsuit against her dealer, Richard Saltoun. The complaint was filed in New York State Supreme Court on July 29, six months after the artist terminated her relationship with Saltoun’s namesake gallery, which operates locations in New York, London, and Rome.

Filed by the 91-year-old artist’s son and attorney-in-fact, Blaise Antin, and her studio, Paranoid Productions, the suit claims that Saltoun “initially purported to agree to return all of the works it held” upon their business separation at the gallery's London location on January 16. News of the lawsuit was first reported by Artnet . 

Saltoun claimed in February that the gallery had returned all of Antin’s works to her family, according to filed documents. However, later that month, the artist’s archivist, citing an inventory produced by Saltoun himself, allegedly discovered that Antin was still missing at least 179 works, the majority of which were still held at the London gallery.
items.t: Eleanor Antin Sues Dealer for Withholding Nearly 200 Works

items.title: Vilcek Foundation Launches Open Call for 2027 Grants Offering $200,000 in Funding to US Nonprofits
items.summary:
This week, the Vilcek Foundation announced its third annual open call for grant applications . The organization invites nonprofits whose work aligns with the foundation’s mission to elevate immigrant contributions in the United States and foster an appreciation for the arts and sciences to apply for funding now through March 31, 2027. 

The foundation will award a total of $200,000 to US-based nonprofits as a part of its 2027 grants cycle. Individual organizations may apply for a grant of up to $20,000.

Strong applications demonstrate both a unique vision and clear plan of action for uplifting immigrants, the arts, or the sciences. The Vilcek Foundation is actively expanding the geographic reach of its grantmaking with the goal of supporting organizations across all US states and select territories. items.title: MoMA Plans First US Ana Mendieta Retrospective in Nearly 25 Years for 2027
items.summary:
Following an acclaimed exhibition at Tate Modern in London, Ana Mendieta will be the subject of yet another super-sized show, this one staged across the pond, at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, where it will run from December 12, 2027, to April 15, 2028.

MoMA’s Mendieta show, titled simply “Ana Mendieta: A Retrospective,” will include around 200 works by the artist, an icon of the feminist art movement, a key performance artist, and a sculptor and filmmaker whose work in those mediums has only increased in popularity over the past couple decades. That makes the show the biggest Mendieta exhibition ever staged in the US, where the Cuban-born artist spent much of her short career.

It’s the first major Mendieta show in the US since one staged in 2004 by curator Olga Viso for the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden (which also visited the Whitney Museum in New York), and the first full-scale Mendieta retrospective mounted in the country since one visited the New Museum in New York in 1987, when the artist was less well-known than she is now. A survey focused solely on Mendieta’s films visited various US institutions in 2016.

But where past Mendieta shows have largely been thematic or centered around her output in a specific medium, the MoMA show is intended as a comprehensive retrospective.

Beverly Adams and Sophie Cavoulacos, the MoMA curators organizing the exhibition, said in an email to ARTnews , “First, and foremost, Ana Mendieta is a great artist, truly brilliant. Beyond making compelling images and objects, the issues that were of interest to her continue to…
items.t: MoMA Plans First US Ana Mendieta Retrospective in Nearly 25 Years for 2027

items.title: With a New Miami Partner, Queer Art Prize Returns Following Four-Year Hiatus After Loss of Corporate Support
items.summary:
The Queer Art Prize, the largest cash award in the US for LGBTQ+ artists, is coming back to life after a four-year absence following the loss of corporate support in 2023 that coincided with a wave of anti-trans backlash. 

The prize has a new partner in Miami-based gallery Visu Contemporary, which will support the prize’s resurrection. The organization will dole out two $20,000 prizes, one for sustained achievement and one for recent work, double the previous amount. Runners-up for the recent work will each receive $5,000. 

In addition to announcing the prize’s return, the nonprofit behind it, Queer | Art, also named the 2026 winner of the Sustained Achievement Award: filmmaker Cheryl Dunye, in recognition of her contributions to Black queer cinema. In her work, Dunye is known to push at the boundaries of filmmaking, with characters addressing the camera and the filmmaker appearing as herself, a genre she has called “Dunyementary.”

The prize comes on the 30th anniversary of her feature film The Watermelon Woman (1996), which won the Teddy Award at the Berlin International Film Festival. She is credited as the first out Black lesbian to ever direct a feature. The Watermelon Woman is widely praised, with Backstage calling it “a landmark indie film.” Her directorial credits also include episodes for television series such as Dear White People , Bridgerton , and Hunting Wives .

items.title: Anti-Monuments to Trump
items.summary:
When Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election, I was in the last place I wanted to be: Washington, DC. Where would I go? I wanted nothing to do with his administration’s empty grandeur. I spent the day at Maya Lin’s Vietnam War Memorial, a dark wound in the earth. In this much more hopeful moment post-midterms, Ed Simon asks a related question: How should memorials remember the MAGA era? He points to historical anti-fascist examples in Germany — and also suggests the bulldozing of Trump’s ballroom to rubble as its own kind of monument. 

Satire’s not a bad strategy to record this era, either. Also today, Greg Werkheiser pens an obituary for the National Historic Preservation Act. The act’s next of kin, the National Register of Historic Places, he writes, “is said to be concerned about its own health.”

Finally, don’t miss the newest installation of Jennifer Samet’s “Beer With a Painter” column. She interviews Ivorian painter Ouattara Watts, who works only at night, when the veil between this world and the next is thinnest. Plus, The Met and the Shanghai Museum are teaming up, just weeks after MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Museum joined forces. They say art imitates life; I just didn’t know that meant we were getting museum oligopolies.

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor 

How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?

Anti-monumentalism responds not with grand equestrian statues or neoclassical columns, but with absence and anxiety, minimalism and melancholy. | Ed Simon

items.title: Valerie Solanas’s obscenely funny Scum Manifesto is an unignorable burst of female outrage | Emily Woof
items.summary:
Before an assassination attempt on Andy Warhol in 1968, Solanas used her fierce writing to confront male supremacy. What can her work teach us about expressing raw anger?

It is exhausting to always express anger constructively and reasonably – especially when what you are angry about is violence, exploitation and the inexcusable appetite of disgusting, powerful, greedy men to gain yet more power.

Could you please be more balanced in how you express yourself? Could you make your objection to the destruction of the world – through violating not only women but also the planet – well, more constructive? Could you be a little less unpleasant in your anger?

items.title: Christie’s Buzzy 20th-Century Sale Totals $626.6 M., with Starry Lots Above $80 M. by Kandinsky and Klimt
items.summary:
At its packed Rockefeller Center saleroom on Tuesday night, Christie’s staged a sometimes lively, sometimes listless two-hour-and-40-minute sale of 20th-century art, led by an $85.8 million abstraction by Wassily Kandinsky, closely followed by an $82.3 million landscape by Gustav Klimt. The house estimated the 74-lot sale to bring $511–$743 million, once adjusted for five works withdrawn before the sale. (Among the withdrawn works was a Frida Kahlo estimated at $2 to $3.5 million, which was pulled just hours before the proceedings were set to begin.) The hammer total for the night came to $521.1 million, slightly above the low estimate. With the house’s fees added, the sale totaled $626.6 million.

Records were set for Hans Bellmer, Fernando Botero, Wassily Kandinsky, Wifredo Lam, and Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem. At the same time, there were some failures to launch: works by Fernand Léger, Henri Matisse, Joan Mitchell, Amedeo Modigliani, Henry Moore, and Jackson Pollock did not sell. Still, the house found buyers for 68 of the 74 lots offered, for a healthy sell-through rate of 92 percent.

In the room were market players who formed a walking power list. Among them were dealers Jeffrey Deitch, Larry Gagosian, Thaddaeus Ropac, Christophe van de Weghe, and Dominique Lévy and Brett Gorvy, as well as advisors including Amy Cappellazzo, Kim Heirston, Laura Paulson, and Jussi Pylkkänen, formerly the house’s global president. Royalty for the night was David Nahmad, whose family offered the Kandinsky. He sat in his customary spot in the front row and was the underbidder on a…
items.t: Christie’s Buzzy 20th-Century Sale Totals $626.6 M., with Starry Lots Above $80 M. by Kandinsky and Klimt

items.title: Seven Works Reportedly from Jeff Koons’s Collection Fetch a Lackluster $104 M. at Christie’s, Led by a $31.2 M. Picasso
items.summary:
Jeff Koons has long been an art collector. As far back as 2010, when the New York Times visited “one of the world’s most famous living artists,” his Upper East Side home held works by artists ranging from the French Realist Gustave Courbet and the Rococo painter Jean-Honoré Fragonard to the Impressionist Édouard Manet and the 16th-century Antwerp painter Quentin Massys. He had generally avoided discussing his collection, the Times wrote, “out of discretion and privacy.”

Collectors and the public are getting another look at that collection this week. Nine works consigned to Christie’s New York came from the artist’s holdings, according to two unnamed industry sources who spoke to the Times this fall. The sources said the house had guaranteed Koons a minimum price and that he planned to plow the proceeds toward his famously expensive art production. (Christie’s has identified the seller only as “a distinguished collector.”)

Seven of the works, grouped under the title “Heroes and Lovers,” were offered at the house’s 20th-century art sale on Tuesday. Together they were estimated at $104 million to $153.5 million. The low end alone is slightly more than the $91.1 million Christie’s got in 2019 for Koons’s own 1986 sculpture Rabbit . The other two works will be offered during the house’s Classic Week next year.

The group did not perform particularly well in the end, hammering for a total of just $87.8 million in total, well shy of the low estimate; with the house’s fees, the group sold for $104 million. No lot exceeded its estimate; four fell short of their low estimates.…
items.t: Seven Works Reportedly from Jeff Koons’s Collection Fetch a Lackluster $104 M. at Christie’s, Led by a $31.2 M. Picasso

items.title: Rare Hilma af Klint Work Heads to Auction
items.summary:
Hilma af Klint, “Ser III No. 5” (1920) (image via Bukowskis ) Welcome to our roundup of daily art news, featuring top stories and timely updates handpicked by Hyperallergic's writers and editors. Have a news tip? Get in touch with us . 

Hilma af Klint Work Heads to Auction Works by the Swedish spiritualist and abstract art pioneer, who asked that her paintings remain unseen for 20 years after her death in 1944, have not come up for auction in more than three decades. That's about to change with the emergence of “ Ser III No. 5 ” (1920) at the Stockholm-based house Bukowskis , which estimates the oil and graphite on canvas will fetch up to 8 million SEK (~$791,000) in its upcoming November 18–19 sale. Controversy has long followed the legacy of the late artist , with some arguing that her works should be kept together rather than sold and commercialized .

Sotheby's Settles Dispute With Heirs Who Contested Van Gogh Sale After the heirs of the Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer requested the withdrawal of Van Gogh's “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (1890) from a sale at Sotheby's, claiming that the work had been sold under duress amid Nazi persecution in Europe, the family has reached a “mutually satisfactory resolution” with the work's consignors, said a Sotheby's statement shared with Hyperallergic. But will the dispute put a damper on sale results? We'll find out tomorrow night when the painting, valued at $180 million, goes under the hammer.
items.t: Rare Hilma af Klint Work Heads to Auction

items.title: How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?
items.summary:
At the intersection of the Harburger Ring and Sand Street in Hamburg, Germany, there is a most unusual public memorial, visible only to those who already know what they’re looking for. 

When the “ Monument Against Fascism ” was unveiled in 1986, it was a 40-foot-tall (~12.2 m) rectangular aluminum pillar covered in lead sheeting on which Hamburg residents were invited to inscribe their own pledges to fight authoritarianism. Over the next seven years, the column was lowered into the ground in stages, so that today the monument is entirely subterranean, visible only through a small glass window next to the plaque. 

Designed by married conceptual artists Esther Shalev-Gerz and Jochen Gerz and commissioned by the Municipal Council of Hamburg-Harburg, the monument was intended to confront both Germany’s Nazi past and the reemergence of far-right politics in a provocative, arresting manner that purposefully eschewed the monumental architecture that fascists themselves exalted. The result was Shalev-Gerz and Gerz’s consummate anti-monument, a reminder that the war against fascism is as personal as someone’s handwriting and as continual as the ground beneath our feet.
items.t: How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?

items.title: Shahzia Sikander Confronts British Colonial Legacy in High Line Video Work
items.summary:
A new joint video exhibition has opened above 14th Street on the High Line, featuring three moving-image works that illustratively dissect and defy the economic legacies of the British Empire's grip on South Asia and China. Screening daily until January 11, Between Salt and Smoke presents two animated videos by Pakistani-American artist Shahzia Sikander and one documented performance by artists Himali Singh Soin and David Soin Tappeser, who make up the duo Hylozoic/Desires. 

The artists examine British colonial extraction and violence in Asia through the lens of the East India Company's monopolies on salt, opium, and other highly valued goods. A new work by Sikander, “3 to 12 Nautical Miles” (2026), consists of hand-painted images that the artist digitally animated in a research-driven cinematic exploration of trade history between the declining Mughal Empire, the East India Company, and the Qing Dynasty. 

Shahzia Sikander, still from “3 to 12 Nautical Miles” (2026) (image courtesy the artist)
items.t: Shahzia Sikander Confronts British Colonial Legacy in High Line Video Work

items.title: Olivia Reavey's Impromptu Sensuality
items.summary:
Olivia Reavey moves at breakneck speed. Her silver-gelatin-analog printing process is frenzied and intense: Black-and-white prints are cut into irregular quadrilaterals with crumpled edges, then hung unframed and loosely fixed to the walls with clips, pins, and other supports. But this is not just slapdash; everything here is intentionally energetic and playful, with images asserting the body’s formal pleasure captured in film.

Many bare their flesh but are often obfuscated or appear with objects: a broken branch covers a male’s buttocks in “Stick” (all works 2026); a wooden lever protrudes from a woman’s pubic area, captured in the reflection of a mirror in “Untitled.” The penetrative and phallic elements here are obvious, but also read neutrally in a recurring tension between eroticism and form — shapes and tonal values outweigh anything provocative. 

Installation view of Olivia Reavey: Distention at Thomas Erben Gallery (photo courtesy Thomas Erben Gallery)
items.t: Olivia Reavey's Impromptu Sensuality

items.title: Meet Natalie White, Photography’s Giant Polaroid Whisperer
items.summary:
Natalie White, “You Should’ve Seen it in Color” (2024), Giant Polaroid (image courtesy the artist) WHATELY, Mass. — The text message said to head around back to the barn, an only slightly ominous-looking structure with heavily weathered wooden siding, tucked off a winding road in Franklin County, Massachusetts. Inside was one of the world’s only 20x24 Polaroid Land Cameras — sometimes referred to as the Giant Polaroid — and the artist Natalie White, shooting with a rapidly dwindling stock of nearly 20-year-old film long past its expiration date.

A muse and model-turned-photographer, performance artist, and feminist activist, White just debuted 15 of her unique large-format Polaroids in Natalie White: Strange Magick , a selling exhibition at Phillips Los Angeles. The images are colorful and dreamy, close-up portraits of the artist with an otherworldly quality. Each photo is a double exposure, an unpredictable process that creates ghostly effects with White’s hands and fingers overlaid atop her face.

To achieve this, White leaves the film in the camera after pushing the shutter, takes a second shot, and hopes for the best. 

“We’re giving all control to the negative,” White told Hyperallergic . “We always joke that there’s a little magical man painting inside the camera who decides what the double exposure is going to look like.”
items.t: Meet Natalie White, Photography’s Giant Polaroid Whisperer

items.title: University of Birmingham pauses plans to move Shakespeare Institute after outcry

The University of Birmingham has paused plans to move its much-loved Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon to its city campus after an outcry from scholars, actors and enthusiasts around the world.

Prof Adam Tickell, the university’s vice-chancellor and principal, issued a statement on Tuesday evening saying proposals to relocate the institute and its renowned 60,000-volume library to the university’s Edgbaston campus would be put on hold while its future was explored.

items.title: The Met and the Shanghai Museum Sign Collaborative Agreement
items.summary:
Fluorescent foliage, crisp breezes, dogs in sweaters, and international museum partnership announcements — one of these is not like the others, but you can check them all off on this autumn's bingo card. The Metropolitan Museum of Art in Manhattan and the Shanghai Museum have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) codifying their relationship ahead of a dual-collection historic jewelry exhibition opening at the Shanghai institution this week. 

The MoU between the two museums was announced less than three weeks after the Museum of Modern Art, Centre Pompidou in Paris, and M+ Museum in Hong Kong publicized their collections alliance at the end of October, further illustrating an institutional shift toward resource pooling, joint acquisitions, and other collaboration initiatives popularized in the wake of pandemic-induced budget deficits. 

The Met and the Shanghai Museum, which have worked together on myriad projects and exhibitions since 1980, stated in a press release that their shared goals in scholarship and presentation advancement will manifest through “exhibitions, research initiatives, and curatorial exchange.”
items.t: The Met and the Shanghai Museum Sign Collaborative Agreement

items.title: Beer With a Painter: Ouattara Watts
items.summary:
Last month, just a couple of weeks before Ouattara Watts’s solo show opened at Karma, I was directed to knock on the cracked glass door of his Bushwick studio. We met in the late afternoon, which is when his studio time begins. The Ivorian-American artist has coffee and a light evening meal, and works all night, before returning home to sleep during the day. To learn why Watts works only at night, one need only look at his paintings. He views art as a portal to the divine; night is when the veil with the spiritual realm is thinnest, and the outside voices of the physical world are quietest. 

Although a gallery representative had told me Watts would be putting “finishing touches” on the paintings for his exhibition at the time of our meeting, I came to realize that he thinks about the work, and his process, without a beginning or end. The centrifugal energy of his rhythmic compositions does not obey edges. Totemic forms continue beyond the bounds of the canvases; arrows point in varying directions; seed pods are split open to reveal concentric circles. His compositions are stained and dripped fields populated by a lexicon of imagery and symbols, developed over the past four decades. They include coffee beans, sacred books, musical notes, serpents, bursting petals encased in atoms, diagrammatic cubes, and mathematical codes. 

Ouattara Watts, “Love Supreme” (2026), mixed media on canvas (© Ouattara Watts; image courtesy the artist and Karma)
items.t: Beer With a Painter: Ouattara Watts

items.title: RIP to the National Historic Preservation Act
items.summary:
The National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), the beloved American law that spent six decades giving communities a voice in federal decisions affecting the places that tell their stories, died shortly after its birthday following a brief but devastating bout of congressional malpractice. It was 60.

Born on October 15, 1966, with unanimous bipartisan support and signed into law by then-President Lyndon B. Johnson, NHPA was conceived in response to a national epidemic of federally sponsored demolition. Americans discovered that an astonishing 50% of the nation’s 12,000 historic buildings and landmarks documented in an inventory begun by the Civil Works Administration in 1933 had been demolished amid federally supported urban renewal and highway development — a breathtaking path of destruction dubbed “ the death mask of America .”

NHPA’s central proposition was modest: Before the federal government or a developer damaged or destroyed an important part of America’s heritage, it simply needed to stop, look, and listen.
items.t: RIP to the National Historic Preservation Act

items.title: Who Gets Remembered in Art History? New Free Online Course Explores Women Who Shaped Indonesian Art
items.summary:
How have women artists shaped Indonesia's cultural, social, and artistic histories? National Gallery Singapore's new free online course, Art and Women in Indonesia: Stories that Empower , co-developed with independent curator Alia Swastika, explores this question through the practices and perspectives of leading contemporary artists.   

Screenshot image from Art as Resistance by National Gallery Singapore (2026) “The absence of women [in historical accounts] does not necessarily indicate a lack of participation.” — Alia Swastika

The course underscores the importance of recovering women’s contributions and bringing overlooked figures and landmark events into view. 

Through the work of artists from different generations, regions, and artistic backgrounds, Art and Women in Indonesia highlights a plurality of experiences and perspectives, offering new ways of understanding Indonesia’s histories and their continued resonance in the present. 

Structured over five weeks, the course explores the practices of six artists and one collective whose work spans painting, sculpture, installation, performances, and collaborative forms. Together, they illuminate the diverse ways women have contributed to Indonesia’s cultural landscape while engaging questions of memory, power, gender, spirituality, and resistance. 

Featured artists include Arahmaiani and Dolorosa Sinaga, whose works confront authoritarianism, censorship, conservatism, and the politics of the female body in public space. Through distinct artistic approaches, they expose the mechanisms through which women’s lives are…
items.t: Who Gets Remembered in Art History? New Free Online Course Explores Women Who Shaped Indonesian Art.

items.title: ‘How can we make it riskier?’: the trans theatre troupe turning Virginia Woolf’s Orlando into a ‘porno-biography’
items.summary:
A radical new take on the modernist classic includes a Berlin ketamine binge, a ‘goon cave’ and an all-trans cast. The manifesto? To ‘desecrate’ expectations

As Orlando’s on a comedown after a ket-heavy night out in Berlin, surrounded by a group of sharp-tongued trans sex workers, Charli Cowgill and Laurie Ward pause the read-through. The scene is new and “it’s feeling a little safe,” Ward says, drumming the table. “How can we make it riskier?”

Cowgill and Ward are piss/CARNATION, a theatre-making duo creating fearless, messy and intellectually rigorous work. Audience spit was collected and thrown in their first production, 52 Monologues for Young Transsexuals, a show that collated trans women’s experiences of men and sex work. Ugly Sisters, the pair’s riotous follow-up, relived a brief encounter between a trans woman and Germaine Greer who wrote a caustic article about it. “As a company,” Ward says, “we tend more towards brutal than twee.”

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘Dolls deserve complex roles’: the trans theatre troupe turning Orlando into a ‘porno-biography’

items.title: Latinx Art’s New Visionaries
items.summary:
Optimism is a rare sight in this day and age — which is why scholar Arlene Dávila’s unabashed excitement about Latinx art right now is so invigorating. These artists draw from vernacular traditions, community histories, family memories, and more to reframe the narrative, despite facing a barrage of attacks in recent years. “The work of these new visionaries is a rallying cry,” she writes in an opinion piece today. “Now is the time to write, create, and make art boldly — together.”

Read on for a pulse on the rest of the art world, from novelist Stephanie Wambugu on Mary Lovelace O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, to Martin Puryear’s quietly revolutionary sculptures, to a new film reevaluating Frida Kahlo’s legacy and commodification. And it wouldn’t be the art world without some auction drama. Today, heirs of the Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer call on Sotheby’s to withdraw a Van Gogh painting it valued at $180 million, alleging that the work was sold under duress during World War II. Meanwhile, at Christie’s, a Willem de Kooning painting that entered the Whitney’s collection just a few years ago is headed under the hammer as Marquee Week kicks off in NYC.

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor 

Latinx Artists Are the New Visionaries

Latinx communities are facing one of the most aggressive series of attacks in recent history, with many families enduring the pain of separation, persecution, and dehumanization. But if you’ve been paying attention to Latinx arts and culture, you’ll see that as we are being told to hide and disappear, artists are stepping into newfound…
items.t: Latinx Art’s New Visionaries

items.title: The play that changed my life: ‘John Berger’s Pig Earth became something magical – they licked milk off bodies’
items.summary:
The Three Lives of Lucie Cabrol by Complicité conjured the struggles of a French village with an intense rawness

There are many things you see that are impactful, but few you can genuinely say change your life. I saw Complicité’s The Three Lives of Lucie Cabrol aged 16 on a school trip to Riverside Studios in London and it really reached me. I’d been educated in a very language, words-based way. Here the story was told – with such intensity! – through people’s bodies.

The world they were conjuring, from a story by John Berger in his book Pig Earth, was about this remote French village – a world of labour. And the strife and struggles of these characters was expressed through the physical work of the company.

items.title: Why Is the Whitney Museum Selling a De Kooning Painting?
items.summary:
Willem de Kooning, “Yellow River” (1958) (image courtesy Christie’s Images Ltd. 2026) Looking to cash in on marquee week in New York, the Whitney Museum of American Art has consigned a Willem de Kooning painting from its collection to Christie's for its 20th-century evening sale tomorrow, November 17. Once a promised gift to the museum, de Kooning's “Yellow River” (1958) is expected to fetch up to $18 million. 

The practice of museum deaccessioning has long been a subject of controversy . In 2022, the Association of Art Museum Directors (AAMD) loosened its policy to allow institutions to apply funds from the sale of deaccessioned art toward the “direct care” of their collections. 

A lot description for “Yellow River” on Christie's website notes that the proceeds will benefit the Whitney's collection. The Whitney has not yet responded to Hyperallergic 's request for comment, but a museum spokesperson told Artnet News that deaccessioning is “a component of the Whitney’s collections strategic plan, allowing the museum to thoughtfully evaluate and refine its holdings in support of its long-term collection priorities.”

The de Kooning painting going under that hammer had a rooted connection to the Whitney before it was bequeathed to the museum in 2023. Postwar art collector, attorney, and museum trustee David Solinger, who would go on to become the museum's first president beyond the Whitney family in 1966, purchased the work from de Kooning's sold-out exhibition at Sidney Janis Gallery in 1959.

items.title: Souped-up and now on screen, Starlight Express is moving in all sorts of ways
items.summary:
Luke Sheppard’s revival of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s 80s musical is in cinemas and going on tour. What gives these ridiculous, rollerskating trains such emotional force?

I hardly ever cry at the theatre but can think of three recent cases. 1. The beautifully jittery balcony scene in Liverpool Everyman’s Romeo and Juliet. 2. Dear Theodosia as co-sung by Leslie Odom Jr (actual OG Aaron Burr!) in Hamilton. 3. An embarrassingly large amount of Starlight Express.

Why on earth does this ridiculous fantasy of rollerskating trains, with their high-speed scrapes, leave me feeling like an emotional wreck? That’s what happened when I first saw director Luke Sheppard’s souped-up London revival – and again this month, watching a new film of that production.

items.summary:
Exclusive: Trailer released for Rambert’s version of Russell T Davies’s show about friendship amid the 80s Aids crisis and the ‘extraordinary freedom’ of clubbing

Russell T Davies’s award-winning series It’s a Sin, about young gay friends living through the Aids crisis in 1980s London, is getting a new life as a dance piece, with a trailer released on Monday ahead of an opening at Aviva Studios in Manchester in February.

“We had a few approaches, but a lot of people wanted to make it a musical, which made my heart sink slightly,” said Davies. “I always imagined an aria between those two women on the seafront at the end and I thought: ‘Oh, that could be so terrible!’” Dance was different, he said. “It felt so original and so pure. The story distils down to these emotional moments that are going to be done so beautifully on stage.”

items.title: Tamsin Greig is sensational in a Cranford where comedy and pain are in perfect balance
items.summary:
Orange Tree theatre, London
This streamlined adaptation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel gets right to the heart of her characters, who face heartbreak and loss but gain from the strength of female friendship

There’s more than one worry for any new dramatisation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel to contend with. There is the risk of this story, set among the unmarried women and widows of a fictional English town, being considered Middlemarch lite – and overshadowed by the Royal Shakespeare Company’s luminous adaptation of the George Eliot novel, currently running in Stratford-Upon-Avon. Then there is the 2007 BBC adaptation of Cranford, which threw every national treasure at it, trowelling on the lovable humour and sentiment as it did so.

This production, however, co-created by Lin Coghlan, Shaun McKenna and Josh Roche, bypasses all those dangers by leaning into theatricality – and sheer good acting. The script is by Coghlan and McKenna, who previously adapted The Forsyte Saga, staged last year by the RSC. They confidently fillet the original and also add their own little inventions.

Continue reading...
items.t: Tamsin Greig is sensational in a Cranford where comedy and pain are in perfect balance
